newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to restore train services to border.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to restore train services to border.

text.p: Bangladesh will restore train services to its southwestern border at Benapole for transporting goods to and from India, reviving a link that lapsed after fighting three decades ago, officials said on Wednesday.
They said the government had decided to open the rail link, which had been suspended since a 1965 war between India and Pakistan.
Bangladesh, formerly East Pakistan, emerged as an independent country following another war in 1971, in which India helped Bengali guerrillas fight the Pakistani army.
The officials said the 34-km (21-mile) rail line linking the southwestern district of Jessore to Benapole was expected to be opened in May next year.
The Bangladesh Railway is trying to arrange 240 million taka ($6 million) needed for buying sleepers and repairing the signalling system, they said.
The link will facilitate direct rail links between the Bangladesh port city of Khulna and Calcutta, capital of India's West Bengal state.

The plan to revive the rail link comes amid speculation that Bangladesh's new government under Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina may accept New Delhi's plea for a land transport route through Bangladesh to serve India's isolated northeastern states.
Railway officials, however, said the link was needed to ease increasing congestion of goods and passengers at Benapole.
Bangladesh, which has about $1.5 billion worth of official and unofficial trade with India a year, uses Benapole for the lion's share of the transactions.
A senior railway official said the state-run Bangladesh Railway would turn into a profitable company if it was allowed to carry Indian goods.

He estimated that only two goods trains running daily between West Bengal and India's northeastern state of Tripura through Bangladesh could earn the Bangladesh Railway at least 600 million taka ($15 million) a year.

Bangladesh's ailing railway sector, with freight and passengers dwindling because of competition from road and ferry services, requires a one billion taka ($25 million) subsidy from the exchequer every year.
"The railway must carry goods from other countries to survive," the railway official said.

With the Calcutta port facing silt problems, the Jessore-Benapole rail link would encourage traders from both India and Nepal to use Bangladesh's second sea port at Mongla, near Khulna, if transit is allowed to India, he said.
